title: AI-Supported Data Analysis Boosts Student Motivation and Reduces Stress in Physics Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether AI-supported data analysis can improve learning and emotional-motivational outcomes in physics education compared with a traditional Excel-based approach. The study is motivated by the growing use of large language models in education and the need for empirical evidence about whether AI tools actually improve student learning, especially in data-intensive physics tasks. The authors focus on three questions: whether students in each condition improve from pre-test to post-test, whether AI leads to greater learning gains than Excel, and whether the two tools differ in their effects on motivation, enjoyment, stress, and related emotional variables.

The intervention compared two ways of analyzing pendulum experiment data: a traditional Microsoft Excel workflow and an AI-supported custom chatbot called ExperiMentor, built on ChatGPT-4o. ExperiMentor was designed to guide students through data analysis using probing questions, contextual hints, formulas, and error-prevention support, while avoiding giving full solutions directly. Both groups completed the same string-pendulum and spring-pendulum evaluation tasks, worked on prepared computers, and took pre- and post-tests that measured conceptual understanding, data-analysis competence, and emotional-motivational responses. Participants were randomly assigned by seat choice to computers configured either with Excel or with the AI tool.

The study was conducted at the University of Cologne in Germany with 50 student teachers preparing for different school types. The sample included 35 Bachelor of Arts students and 15 Master of Education students, making the population primarily undergraduate and graduate pre-service educators in a university physics-education context. The intervention appears to have taken place in an in-person computer-based instructional/lab setting. Objective performance was assessed through multiple-choice items on pendulum physics and data evaluation, while emotional and motivational constructs were measured using Likert-scale surveys.

The main findings show that both groups improved, but the AI group showed larger within-group gains, especially in spring-pendulum and data-evaluation tasks. However, between-group comparisons did not show statistically significant differences in overall learning gains, suggesting that AI was not clearly superior to Excel in quantitative achievement over this short intervention. The strongest advantages of the AI condition were qualitative: students using ExperiMentor reported greater enjoyment, motivation, positive emotional experience, perceived method effectiveness, and lower stress, frustration, and uncertainty than students using Excel. The authors conclude that AI tools such as custom chatbots may not automatically produce stronger immediate learning gains than conventional tools, but they can create a more motivating and emotionally supportive learning environment for physics data analysis.

identified_tools.name: ExperiMentor
identified_tools.description: A custom GPT chatbot built on ChatGPT for physics experimental data analysis using Python. It gives contextual hints, relevant formulas, probing questions, and error-prevention support while avoiding direct solution paths.
identified_tools.use_case: Used by student teachers in a randomized pre-post control-group study to analyze string and spring pendulum datasets and support physics data analysis, compared against Microsoft Excel.

findings.finding_summary: Within the AI group, total performance improved significantly from pre-test M=7.64 (SD=3.43) to post-test M=9.92 (SD=2.96). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test was significant (p=5.8∙10^-5) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d=1.4537).
findings.measure: Pre-post total score across all physics concept and data analysis items

findings.finding_summary: For the AI group, spring pendulum performance increased from M=1.40 (SD=1.29) to M=2.20 (SD=1.29), with a significant pre-post change (p=0.0039). The reported effect size was medium-to-large (Cohen’s d=0.7407).

The AI group showed significant gains in data evaluation, rising from M=3.00 (SD=1.61) to M=4.00 (SD=1.22). This pre-post change was significant (p=0.0009) with a large effect size (Cohen’s d=0.9258).

Post-intervention, the AI group reported higher positive emotional learning experience than the Excel group (AI M=2.26 vs Excel M=1.74). The Wilcoxon rank-sum test showed a significant difference (p=0.0156) with a moderate effect size (d=0.75).

The AI group reported lower negative emotional learning experience than the Excel group (AI M=0.64 vs Excel M=1.56). This difference was highly significant (p<0.0001) with a very large negative effect size (d=-1.47), indicating less stress, uncertainty, and frustration with the AI-supported method.

Participants using the AI-supported method rated the method more favorably than Excel users on Perception of Methods (AI M=2.44 vs Excel M=1.68). The difference was highly significant (p<0.0001) with a very large effect size (d=1.35).
The AI group rated Method Effectiveness higher than the Excel group (AI M=2.52 vs Excel M=1.88). This between-group difference was significant (p=0.0043) with a large effect size (d=0.95).

Motivation was higher in the AI group than in the Excel group after the intervention (AI M=2.28 vs Excel M=1.56). The Wilcoxon test indicated a highly significant difference (p=0.0003) with a very large effect size (d=1.17).

Between groups, overall learning gains did not differ significantly despite somewhat higher raw gains in the AI group. ANCOVA for total score was non-significant (p=0.3924), and the Hake index was low for both groups (AI g=0.0244; Excel g=0.0132).
findings.measure: Between-group difference in total learning gains

findings.finding_summary: Self-reported perceived learning gains did not significantly differ between AI and Excel conditions (AI M=1.38 vs Excel M=1.26). The Wilcoxon test was non-significant (p=0.6580) with a small effect size (d=0.2005).

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s ChatGPT family of large language models used here as the base model underlying the custom GPT system.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper states that ExperiMentor was developed based on ChatGPT-4o; ChatGPT is referenced as the underlying platform rather than separately evaluated as an independent intervention.

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical randomized pre-post control-group study with n=50 and a comparison condition, but it is small-sample and reports some measurement limitations and non-normal data concerns. That places it below the strongest causal evidence tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports several medium-to-large and very large effect sizes for motivation, emotional experience, perceived method quality, and within-group learning gains for the AI condition, even though between-group academic differences were not significant.
